power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. text.text: Researchers commonly manipulate chatbot anthropomorphism through social cues, whose effects vary and may introduce unintended perceptual differences.
Generative AI enables an alternative: manipulating perceived characteristics through natural-language prompting.
Two online experiments (N = 84 each) evaluated behavior-prescriptive and perception-goal prompting for manipulating anthropomorphism.
Study 1 found no significant differences in anthropomorphism.
Study 2 found significant differences in general, mindful, and mindless anthropomorphism (ds = .86-.95), without significant differences in response coherence or perceived intelligence.

These findings provide initial empirical support for perception-goal prompting and suggest broader methodological possibilities for manipulating perceived chatbot characteristics in human-AI communication research.
Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly integrated into everyday communication contexts, such as customer service and health care. (Adam et al., 2021; Laymouna et al., 2024).

text.text: One important feature of AI chatbots that can influence users' reactions is anthropomorphism, defined as the attribution of humanlike characteristics to nonhuman agents (Epley et al., 2007).

text.text: However, these manipulations may also influence perceptions beyond anthropomorphism, such as perceived identity and perceived social distance, which makes it difficult to attribute observed effects to anthropomorphism itself.
Prompting Large language models (LLMs) offers an alternative: researchers can guide a chatbot's communication through natural-language instructions.

Yet it remains unclear whether prompt-based manipulations can effectively manipulate anthropomorphism in generative AI, and whether they do so without introducing unintended differences in other perceptions.
The present research addresses this challenge through two experiments examining behavior-prescriptive prompting and perception-goal prompting.

Specifically, this study tested whether these two approaches successfully manipulate users' perceived anthropomorphism and whether they alter response coherence and perceived intelligence, unintentionally.
In doing so, this research seeks to provide methodological guidance for experimentally manipulating anthropomorphism in AI chatbots.
Scholars have conceptualized anthropomorphism as a tendency, a process, a technological feature, or a perception (Li & Suh, 2021).
text.formatted: Scholars have conceptualized anthropomorphism as a tendency, a process, a technological feature, or a perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Li & Suh, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Classic work describes it as the "tendency to imbue the real or imagined behavior of nonhuman agents with humanlike characteristics, motivations, intentions, or emotions" (Epley et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Classic work describes it as the "tendency to imbue the real or imagined behavior of nonhuman agents with humanlike characteristics, motivations, intentions, or emotions" <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Epley et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The present research adopts the perceptual perspective, emphasizing users' subjective perceptions of an AI chatbot as humanlike.
More specifically, scholars distinguish anthropomorphism into mindful and mindless anthropomorphism, representing two distinct modes through which users perceive agents as humanlike.

Mindful anthropomorphism refers to the deliberate and thoughtful attribution of human traits and characteristics to the media agent, whereas mindless anthropomorphism refers to the non-conscious, intuitive, and spontaneous attribution of such traits and characteristics (Nass & Moon, 2000; Kim & Sundar, 2012; Lombard & Xu, 2021).

text.text: Researchers have manipulated chatbot anthropomorphism through visual and identityrelated cues, such as humanlike avatars and names (Go & Sundar, 2019; Seeger et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023), and communicative cues, such as informal language (Araujo, 2018), first-person pronouns, small talk, and empathetic expressions (Adam et al., 2021), humor, and humanlike response delays (Schanke et al., 2021).

text.text: These cues are frequently combined to create anthropomorphic chatbots.
However, their effectiveness varies. Reuter et al.'s (2025) scoping review showed that these cues can perform successful, partially successful, and unsuccessful anthropomorphism manipulation.

text.text: More broadly, Klein's (2025) meta-analysis found a small positive overall effect of humanlike cues on users' social responses, with variation across outcomes and interaction conditions.
The inconsistent success of existing manipulations motivates exploring additional approaches to eliciting perceived anthropomorphism (Reuter et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The inconsistent success of existing manipulations motivates exploring additional approaches to eliciting perceived anthropomorphism <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Reuter et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Changes to appearance or communication style may also influence other chatbot evaluations, making it harder to isolate effects attributable to anthropomorphism.
These considerations encourage communication scholars to explore alternative manipulation approaches.
Generative AI provides additional possibilities for implementing such manipulations.

Powered by large language models, generative AI chatbots are able to generate responses using patterns learned from extensive training data and the ongoing conversational context (Shanahan et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Powered by large language models, generative AI chatbots are able to generate responses using patterns learned from extensive training data and the ongoing conversational context <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Shanahan et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Their responses can be guided through natural-language instructions, allowing researchers to specify communicative behaviors or intended characteristics while retaining flexibility to respond to individual messages (Lin, 2024).
text.formatted: Their responses can be guided through natural-language instructions, allowing researchers to specify communicative behaviors or intended characteristics while retaining flexibility to respond to individual messages <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Lin, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This capability makes prompting a promising approach to manipulating chatbot anthropomorphism during real-time interaction.
Behavior-prescriptive prompting specifies communicative behaviors that a chatbot should perform or avoid to elicit anthropomorphism.
Researchers can translate established anthropomorphic cues into instructions, such as using first-person pronouns or a conversational tone.
This approach offers explicit control over which social cues appear.
However, rigid prescriptions may compromise conversational flexibility and make responses less responsive to individual messages.
Perception-goal prompting specifies how users should perceive the chatbot.
For example, researchers can instruct a chatbot to ensure that users perceive it as humanlike by the end of the interaction.
This approach allows communicative behaviors to vary with individual messages, potentially supporting more contextual interaction.
However, the specific behaviors that produce the intended perception are less controlled by researchers and may vary across users.
Both approaches can be implemented within a structured prompt that follows the CO-STAR framework, which specifies context, objective, style, tone, audience, and response format (Teo, 2023).

text.text: To make the results comparable, researchers should hold all factors outside the intended manipulation constant, including the task objective, response-length instructions, and information-source requirements, by specifying them identically in each prompt.
Technical settings, including the model version, generation parameters, and maximum output length, should likewise remain consistent across conditions.
These shared specifications help limit unintended variation while preserving the targeted contrast.

To evaluate whether these two approaches can successfully manipulate anthropomorphism, the present research asks: RQ1: Do behavior-prescriptive prompting and perception-goal prompting each produce differences in general, mindful, and mindless anthropomorphism between anthropomorphic and non-anthropomorphic chatbot conditions?
Evaluating prompt-based anthropomorphism manipulations also requires examining whether other chatbot perceptions vary between conditions.
Two relevant evaluations are response coherence and perceived intelligence.
Response coherence refers to the degree to which the AI chatbot's outputs are informative, relevant, specific, and clear (Xiao et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Response coherence refers to the degree to which the AI chatbot's outputs are informative, relevant, specific, and clear <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Xiao et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Perceived intelligence concerns users' assessments of the chatbot's functional cognitive capabilities, including its ability to understand requests and provide useful responses (Moussawi et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Perceived intelligence concerns users' assessments of the chatbot's functional cognitive capabilities, including its ability to understand requests and provide useful responses <ref type="bibr">(Moussawi et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Instructions prescribing communicative behaviors or intended perceptions may also affect how clearly or competently the chatbot appears to respond.
Assessing these evaluations therefore helps identify other perceptual differences that could complicate interpretations of the manipulation's effects.

Thus, the present research asks: RQ2: Do behavior-prescriptive prompting and perception-goal prompting each produce differences in response coherence or perceived intelligence between anthropomorphic and nonanthropomorphic chatbot conditions?
Two online experiments evaluated distinct approaches to manipulating anthropomorphism in generative AI chatbots.
Study 1 examined behavior-prescriptive prompting, which specified communicative behaviors the chatbot should perform or avoid.
Study 2 examined perception-goal prompting, which specified how users should perceive the chatbot while allowing flexibility in generating responses toward those perceptions.
Both experiments originally included anthropomorphic chatbot, non-anthropomorphic chatbot, and static-message conditions.
The present analyses focus on the two chatbot conditions.
Participants were recruited through Prolific on March 29 and April 8, 2026, for Studies 1 and 2, respectively.
Eligible participants were U.S. residents aged 21 years or older who had a Prolific approval rate of at least 98% and were current e-cigarette users.
Current use was defined as having used e-cigarettes within the past 30 days without already quitting (Cuccia et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Current use was defined as having used e-cigarettes within the past 30 days without already quitting <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cuccia et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Participants received $2.70 in Study 1 and $2.25 in Study 2 for completing the approximately 15-minute study.
After eligibility screening and informed consent, participants reported their vaping behavior and perceptions and were randomly assigned to a condition.
Participants completed three rounds of vaping-related interaction through an online survey integrated with the OpenAI API.
Both studies used GPT-4.1-mini, with condition-specific instructions supplied to the chatbot API before the interaction.

Participants subsequently completed measures of perceived anthropomorphism, response coherence, perceived intelligence, additional outcomes collected for the broader project, and demographic characteristics before receiving a debriefing.
Full system prompts are provided in supplementary materials.
Study 1 evaluated whether prescribing specific communicative behaviors would produce differences in perceived anthropomorphism.
The anthropomorphic prompt instructed the chatbot to perform designated behaviors, whereas the non-anthropomorphic prompt instructed it to avoid anthropomorphic behaviors.
For example, an instruction in the anthropomorphic condition stated, "Always use first-and second-person singular pronouns (I, me, my, you, your)."

text.text: This approach operationalized the manipulation through instructions governing how the chatbot should communicate.
Of the 85 participants assigned to the chatbot conditions, one failed an attention check and was excluded.
The final analytic sample comprised 84 participants: 43 in the anthropomorphic condition and 41 in the non-anthropomorphic condition.
Study 2 evaluated whether specifying the intended perceptions of the chatbot would produce differences in anthropomorphism.

The anthropomorphic prompt explicitly incorporated the seven attributes used to measure anthropomorphism as the perception goal of the interaction: "The person interacting with you should perceive you as very human-like, natural, lifelike, likeable, sociable, friendly, and personally engaged."
In contrast, the non-anthropomorphic prompt instructed, "Your responses should feel like they come from a system, not a person."
Although these prompts included general behavioral guidance, their organizing principle was the intended perception of the chatbot.
Of the 86 nonpreview participants assigned to the chatbot conditions, two failed an attention check and were excluded.
The final analytic sample comprised 84 participants, with 42 in each condition.
Both studies used vaping cessation as the health-communication context.

Shared instructions directed the chatbots to provide information about vaping risks and cessation strategies, limit responses to 120-150 words, use information consistent with NIH, CDC, or FDA guidance, and avoid diagnosis or medical advice.
Mindful Anthropomorphism and Mindless Anthropomorphism were measured using items adapted from Nass and Moon (2000).

text.text: Mindful anthropomorphism was assessed with three 7point semantic differential items (e.g., machinelike -humanlike).

Mindless anthropomorphism was assessed using four 7-point Likert-type items capturing perceived likability, sociability, friendliness, and personalness, with responses ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
General anthropomorphism was calculated by averaging all seven items.
Higher scores indicated greater perceived anthropomorphism.
Response coherence and perceived intelligence measured additional chatbot evaluations that could vary alongside the anthropomorphism manipulation.
Response coherence was assessed with four 7-point items capturing the informativeness, relevance, specificity, and clarity of the chatbot's responses (Xiao et al., 2020).

The present research evaluated two approaches to manipulating anthropomorphism in real-time interactions with generative AI chatbots.

Addressing RQ1, behavior-prescriptive prompting did not produce significant differences in general, mindful, or mindless anthropomorphism in Study 1, whereas perception-goal prompting produced large differences across all three measures in Study 2.
Addressing RQ2, neither study revealed statistically significant condition differences in response coherence or perceived intelligence.

Together, these findings identify perception-goal prompting as a promising approach for eliciting differences in perceived chatbot anthropomorphism while highlighting the importance of validating promptbased manipulations.
A plausible explanation for these results concerns the flexibility afforded to the chatbot during interaction.
In Study 1, the behavior-prescriptive prompt required the chatbot to follow specific instructions, such as using personal pronouns and engaging in small talk.
Repeatedly applying these behaviors may have produced formulaic responses that limited humanlike impressions.
In contrast, the perception-goal prompt in Study 2 specified the intended perceptions while leaving the choice of communicative behaviors to the chatbot.
This flexibility may have allowed the chatbot to generate more context-sensitive responses tailored to each conversation, thereby more effectively evoking anthropomorphism.

The results for response coherence and perceived intelligence suggest that perceptiongoal prompting elicited differences in anthropomorphism without producing significant differences in these two chatbot evaluations.
However, the difference in response coherence approached the threshold of statistical significance (p = .052).
Future research should continue to assess these variables to better isolate the effects of anthropomorphism.
This research makes one significant contribution.

It introduces perception-goal prompting as an alternative to embedding social cues for manipulating chatbot anthropomorphism, and provides initial evidence that it can produce large and consistent differences in general, mindful, and mindless anthropomorphism.

Beyond anthropomorphism, this approach offers a broader methodological framework for manipulating perceived chatbot characteristics, such as empathy, authoritativeness, and intelligence, by specifying desired perceptions.
There are several limitations.

First, both studies used modest sample sizes, which, although adequate for detecting medium effects (Wilson VanVoorhis & Morgan, 2001), provide limited power for detecting smaller differences in response coherence or perceived intelligence.

text.text: Larger samples would allow more sensitive tests of unintended perceptual differences.
Second, both studies used vaping cessation as the health-communication context, current e-cigarette users as participants, and a single generative model (GPT-4.1-mini).
Generalizing the effectiveness of perception-goal prompting to other topics, populations, and models requires further testing.

Across two experiments, behavior-prescriptive prompting did not produce significant differences in perceived anthropomorphism, whereas perception-goal prompting produced large differences in general, mindful, and mindless anthropomorphism without significant differences in response coherence or perceived intelligence.
These findings highlight the potential of perception-goal prompting as a methodological tool for human-AI communication research.
